traveler: Indra Devi (Eugenia Vasilievna Peterson, Eugenie Strakaty)
title: The Forgotten Call: Riga to Buenos Aires by way of Mysore
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Riga, Petrograd, and the Road West

stops.name: Riga, born in a banker's house
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date and city given by en.wikipedia, 'Indra Devi', by Hinduism Today's 2002 obituary and by Live History India. The parents' names and occupations come from en.wikipedia; the Russian Orthodox baptism from Hinduism Today. The tradition that she kept the baptismal cross all her life is dossier material and is not confirmed by any source reached in this pass.
stops.campa: In the Governorate of Livonia, in a house kept by Vasili Peterson, a Swedish bank director, a daughter is born to his wife Aleksandra Labunskaia, a Russian noblewoman who acts at the Nezlobina Theatre. They christen her Eugenia in the Orthodox rite. The city around her keeps German in its guildhalls, Latvian in its markets, Russian in its offices and Yiddish on its stages. Her mother acts in the Russian one. The empire that governs all four has eighteen years left to run.
suggested_refs: The Nezlobina Theatre company, where her mother acted
Riga parish registers of the Russian Orthodox church, 1899
sources: livehistoryindia.com, 'How Eugenie Peterson (Indra Devi) Took Yoga Global'

stops.name: Petrograd, the gold medal and a book about yoga
stops.date_confidence: attested for the graduation: en.wikipedia gives 1917, Saint Petersburg, with a gold medal. The month is set to June as the ordinary end of the school year and is not itself sourced. The story of the yoga book read at about fifteen comes from the Russian magazine Vokrug Sveta, a popular retelling that names no primary document. Note a lens conflict in the research pool: the same graduation was tagged both attested and unverified by different passes over the same Wikipedia sentence.
stops.campa: The family moves east to the capital during the war, and Eugenia finishes gymnasium there with a gold medal in a city where the bread queues have already brought down a tsar. Somewhere in these years a book about yoga reaches her hands and she reads it the way other girls read novels, over and over, out of order. She is about fifteen. She has met no Indian, cannot place Mysore on a map, and has no reason on earth to think the book concerns her. The magazine that prints the story sixty years later does not say what the book was, or who wrote it, or where she found it.
stops.quote: Йога! Индия! Я должна туда обязательно поехать
stops.quote_source: Her recalled reaction at about fifteen to a book on yoga, as printed in Vokrug Sveta magazine, article no. 7175. 'Yoga! India! I absolutely must go there.' A popular-magazine retelling; no original manuscript is cited on the page.
suggested_refs: The gymnasium leaving certificate of 1917, not located

stops.name: Moscow, the drama school
stops.date_confidence: partly attested. en.wikipedia says she 'briefly attended drama school in Moscow,' which sources the fact of theatrical study but not the year, the school, or the teacher. The common attribution to Fyodor Komissarzhevsky's studio, and the anecdote in which he predicts stardom for her, are unconfirmed by anything reached this pass. The date is set to 1918 to order the segment.
stops.campa: She goes to Moscow to learn the stage, briefly, in the winter the old order finishes collapsing. Which studio took her is not recorded in anything that can be checked; the name attached to it by later tellings is Komissarzhevsky's, and the tellings add that he foresaw a great actress. What she leaves with is a stage training, and that training is the only marketable thing she carries out of Russia. No enrolment list from the Moscow studios of those years has been found.
suggested_refs: Enrolment records of the Moscow theatrical studios, 1917-1920, not located

stops.name: Warsaw, the refugee crossing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The family's flight from the revolution is attested in outline by en.wikipedia, which places her in Berlin by 1921; Hinduism Today gives 1920 as the year she left Russia. The Warsaw leg, the month, and the detail that she travelled with her mother are dossier material with no independently fetched source this pass.
stops.campa: Mother and daughter go west out of the Baltic with what they can carry, through Poland, in the last winter of the Russian civil war. Nothing about the crossing is spiritual. It is a dispossession: a bank director's household reduced to luggage, papers, and whatever the daughter can earn with her face and her voice. The route is uncorroborated in every source that can be checked. Only the direction is attested, and the direction is west. Nobody in the family is making a plan for a return.
suggested_refs: Polish transit records for Russian refugees, winter 1920-1921, not located

stops.name: Berlin, the emigre stage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move: en.wikipedia gives 1921 and Berlin. The claim that she toured with the Russian cabaret company Der Blaue Vogel is dossier material; the source cited for it in the research pool, livehistoryindia, does not mention the company at all. The company is real; her membership in it is not confirmed here.
stops.campa: Weimar Berlin holds tens of thousands of Russians who arrived the way she did, and it grows theatres to match. Eugenia works among them as an actress and a dancer, in a language that is not the city's, for audiences of other exiles. She is trained, and she is stateless. Later accounts put her in the Blue Bird company, the cabaret that carried Russian material through Berlin and on to Paris and London; the accounts are repeated everywhere and documented nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: Programmes of Der Blaue Vogel (The Blue Bird) Russian cabaret, Berlin, 1921-1928
sources: livehistoryindia.com, 'How Eugenie Peterson (Indra Devi) Took Yoga Global'

stops.name: Ommen, the fire at the Star camp
stops.date_confidence: attested for the encounter and the year: es.wikipedia states she met Jiddu Krishnamurti in 1926 during one of his talks at Ommen, Holland. A contradiction is left standing: livehistoryindia instead places the encounter in Berlin in the 1920s, and attaches the same recollection to it. The month is set to August, when the annual camps were held. A nomenclature point: in 1926 the body was still the Order of the Star in the East, renamed the Order of the Star only in June 1927. The pin is inherited from jiddu_krishnamurti.journey.json for the Eerde estate at Ommen.
stops.campa: On the Eerde estate near Ommen, thousands camp under the Dutch trees for the annual gathering of the Order of the Star in the East. Jiddu Krishnamurti, raised since boyhood as the vehicle of a world teacher, chants Sanskrit at the fire, and a twenty-seven-year-old Russian actress with no Sanskrit at all sits and listens to it. She will describe the next hour, for the rest of her life, as the hinge of her existence. Where that hour happened is disputed: one account moves it to Berlin, in the same decade, with the same recollection attached to it.
stops.quote: It seemed to me, I was hearing a forgotten call, familiar, but distant. From that day everything in me turned upside down.
stops.quote_source: Quoted via Elliott Goldberg, The Path of Modern Yoga (2016), pp. 338-339, in the Wikipedia article 'Indra Devi'; independently echoed in Live History India. Goldberg's own pages were not reached in this pass.
suggested_refs: The Eerde estate near Ommen, given to the Order of the Star in the East in 1923
Elliott Goldberg, The Path of Modern Yoga (2016), pp. 338-339
sources: livehistoryindia.com, 'How Eugenie Peterson (Indra Devi) Took Yoga Global'

stops.name: Berlin, the bargain with Hermann Bolm
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The engagement to the banker Hermann Bolm, the condition that she see India first, and his funding of the voyage in the expectation that it would cure her come from her own retrospective account as relayed by the dossier and by Vokrug Sveta. No source reached this pass confirms Bolm independently; his papers have not been consulted by anyone.
stops.campa: A banker named Hermann Bolm asks her to marry him. She answers that she will, on one condition: that she see India first, once, and get it out of her system. He pays for the passage, on exactly that understanding, because a three-month voyage is cheaper than a lifetime of the subject. Every element of this scene reaches the record through Devi herself, decades later, telling a story she had by then told many times, and no ledger, letter or ticket survives to check it against.
suggested_refs: Hermann Bolm's papers, not located

stops.name: Bombay, first landfall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: livehistoryindia and the Dawn obituary both give an India journey beginning in 1927. The exact sailing date of 17 November, the south-to-north route, and the three-month duration come from her own retrospective account and are not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: She lands in Bombay at twenty-eight with a return ticket a German banker has paid for. She goes south to north across the country in the months that follow, and finds that the thing she had recognised at a fire in the Netherlands is here in ordinary daylight, in temples, on roads, in the way strangers speak about the soul over food. The return ticket is still valid and she uses it. She sails for Europe in a sari, having bought one in Bombay and stopped wearing anything else.
suggested_refs: Passenger lists of the Europe-Bombay mail steamers, autumn 1927, not located
sources: livehistoryindia.com, 'How Eugenie Peterson (Indra Devi) Took Yoga Global'

stops.name: Berlin, the ring given back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The breaking of the engagement on her return, and the words she is said to have used, come from Vokrug Sveta's popular retelling, which names no primary source. The month is set to spring 1928 only to order the segment against the 1927 departure.
stops.campa: She comes back to Berlin as agreed, roughly three months later, and gives Bolm his ring. The cure has failed in the way cures fail when the disease was the patient's own nature. She has no money, no country, no profession beyond the stage, and a fixed intention to return to a place where she knows almost nobody. Her mother argues, and her friends argue, and Bolm, who paid for the cure, is left holding the receipt for it. She sells what she has in Berlin and books the passage.
stops.quote_source: Reported in Vokrug Sveta magazine, article no. 7175, as her answer on returning the engagement ring: 'That is my home.' Popular retelling; underlying primary source not named on the page.

stops.name: Berlin, the second departure
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a contradiction stands inside it. Vokrug Sveta prints the exchange with her mother as a dialogue and sets it in Petersburg, which cannot be the scene of a 1928 departure by a woman who left Russia in 1920; either the setting or the date is wrong in that retelling, and no other source carries the exchange at all. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The second voyage is not an experiment. She is going to stay, and everyone who loves her says so out loud, in the tone people use for a decision they cannot reverse. Her mother asks who she has in India. The answer is nobody, and the answer settles nothing, because the question was never about company. What she has is a booking and an hour at a fire in Holland that she has not been able to put down. She leaves Europe at twenty-nine and does not live in it again.
stops.quote_source: Exchange with her mother, printed as a two-turn dialogue in Vokrug Sveta magazine, article no. 7175: 'India... who do you have there?' / 'No one.' The magazine sets the scene in Petersburg; see date_confidence.

segments.name: India, and the Name She Keeps

stops.name: Adyar, the Society's headquarters
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Devi's presence at the Theosophical Society's Adyar headquarters comes from the dossier; neither Time nor Hinduism Today, cited for it in the research pool, mentions Adyar. Her entry into the Theosophical and Krishnamurti network after 1926 is well attested in general terms; this particular ground is not. The pin is the canonical Adyar coordinate inherited from blavatsky.journey.json, annie_besant.journey.json and jiddu_krishnamurti.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Society whose Order she followed to Ommen keeps its world headquarters at Adyar, south of Madras, and Annie Besant, its president, is the most consequential European woman in Indian public life. Eugenia arrives into that milieu with a dancer's training and no doctrine, learns Indian dance, and performs it. Her teacher Enakshi Rama Rau tells her, when she asks to be taught, that there is nothing to teach her. Whether she ever stood on the Adyar sand is a gap in the record, not a fact.
stops.quote: Вы и так все это уже знаете
stops.quote_source: Attributed to her dance teacher Enakshi Rama Rau, addressing her, inside Devi's own retrospective narrative as printed in Vokrug Sveta magazine, article no. 7175: 'You already know all this.' The speaker is Rau, not Devi.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society headquarters at Adyar, Madras
Krishnamurti's dissolution of the Order of the Star at Ommen, 3 August 1929, before Besant and some three thousand members
sources: research dossier synthesis, unconfirmed for Adyar

stops.name: Bombay, the name on the screen
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. en.wikipedia gives 1930 and the film Sher-e-Arab as the occasion of the stage name Indra Devi; that is the only support. Time, cited for it in the research pool, mentions no film and no stage name. The IMDb record returned HTTP 403 and no encyclopaedia article on the film exists, so the director attribution to Bhagwati Prasad Mishra could not be checked at all. Other silent-era credits to an 'Indira Devi' are unresolved and are not claimed here.
stops.campa: Indian silent cinema is hungry for European faces that will work in an Indian frame, and hers does. She is cast in Sher-e-Arab, and for the credits she takes a name out of the country she has adopted: Indra Devi. Eugenia Peterson of Riga is retired at thirty. The screen career lasts a handful of pictures. The name outlives it by seventy-two years and ends up on her passport. No print of Sher-e-Arab is known to survive, and the film record for it could not be opened this pass.
suggested_refs: Sher-e-Arab (The Arabian Knight), 1930, silent; no surviving print located
IMDb record tt0241947, inaccessible (HTTP 403)

stops.name: Bombay, marriage to Jan Strakaty
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage, the year and the husband's post: en.wikipedia gives 1930 and describes Jan Strakaty as Czechoslovak commercial attache in Bombay. Time, cited for this in the research pool, does not mention him. The month is an ordering device, and the claim that he was about forty is unsourced in anything reached this pass.
stops.campa: She marries Jan Strakaty, commercial attache of Czechoslovakia at Bombay, and the stateless refugee becomes a diplomat's wife with a diplomat's passport and a place at a diplomat's table. She is thirty-one and carrying papers from a state she has never lived in, issued by a country that did not exist when she was born. What follows is a decade of consulates and receptions, and postings that move the household first to Mysore and then to Shanghai.
suggested_refs: Czechoslovak consular records for Bombay, 1930s, not consulted

stops.name: Bombay, the attache's wife and the illness
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Bombay diplomatic years are implied by the attested 1930 marriage, but the illness that precedes her turn to yoga is known only from her own memoir account, which Michelle Goldberg's biography treats as partly self-mythologising. Her phrase for the friendship with Jawaharlal Nehru rests on a single popular magazine, Vokrug Sveta; two sources cited for a Nehru connection in the research pool, Time and Hinduism Today, do not mention him at all. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: For most of a decade she is a hostess. The house fills with Indian politicians and European officials at the same hour, which in Bombay in the 1930s is not a neutral arrangement, and among the Indians is Jawaharlal Nehru, for whom she later finds a two-word Russian phrase and no further explanation. Her heart begins troubling her in these years, doctors in three countries can name nothing, and rest does not touch it. She is told the condition has no cure available to her.
stops.quote_source: Her own phrase for the relationship with Jawaharlal Nehru, printed in Vokrug Sveta magazine, article no. 7175: 'an amorous friendship.' Single popular-magazine sourcing only.
suggested_refs: Michelle Goldberg, The Goddess Pose (Knopf, 2015), on the memoir account of the illness

stops.name: Mysore Palace, the Maharaja overrules the teacher
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the intervention. Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV's patronage of Krishnamacharya from 1926 is attested in pattabhi_jois.journey.json, from which this Amba Vilas pin is inherited byte for byte. That the Maharaja personally overruled Krishnamacharya's refusal to teach a foreign woman is a dossier claim, repeated in the yoga literature and confirmed by no source reached this pass. The month and year order the segment against the 1937-or-1938 admission.
stops.campa: Krishnamacharya teaches under the patronage of Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV, who found him, installed him, and pays for the school. When a European woman applies to be taught, the teacher refuses her: she is foreign, she is a woman, and the discipline is not hers. The refusal is overturned from above by the man who signs the cheques. That, at least, is how the story is always told, in the yoga literature and by Devi's own school. Who told it first, and to whom, and whether anyone present at the palace ever wrote it down, nobody has established.
suggested_refs: The patronage of Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV over Krishnamacharya from 1926, at Amba Vilas
sources: research dossier synthesis, unconfirmed for the intervention

stops.name: Jaganmohan Palace, the yogashala
stops.date_confidence: attested that she studied under Tirumalai Krishnamacharya at Mysore and is described as his first foreign woman pupil: en.wikipedia gives 1938, Hinduism Today places her 'under Sri Krishnamacharya at the Maharaja of Mysore's palace' with B. K. S. Iyengar and K. Pattabhi Jois as fellow students. Sources differ between 1937 and 1938. The pin is the yogashala coordinate inherited from pattabhi_jois.journey.json, where the school's opening on 11 August 1933 is recorded; note that this is the Jaganmohan Palace, not Amba Vilas, about two hundred metres away.
stops.campa: The school occupies a wing of the Jaganmohan Palace, and the regimen is austere: diet prescribed and enforced, breath before posture, no allowance made for a European constitution or a middle-aged one. She is thirty-eight. In the same rooms in the same years are K. Pattabhi Jois and B. K. S. Iyengar, boys beside her, and the three of them will carry one teacher's method to three continents without ever agreeing on what it was. Krishnamacharya tells her, when she has finished, to go and teach.
stops.quote: Like water which can clearly mirror the sky and the trees only so long as its surface is undisturbed, the mind can only reflect the true image of the Self when it is tranquil and wholly relaxed.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to Devi on quotation aggregators; no book, edition or page could be traced this pass, and the Internet Archive scans of her books are access-restricted. Reproduced here as tradition, not as a located text.
suggested_refs: The yogashala opened at the Jaganmohan Palace, 11 August 1933
Krishnamacharya's instruction that yoga is a method for physical, mental and spiritual development, not a religion

segments.name: Shanghai, the War, and the First Book

stops.name: Shanghai, teaching at Soong Mei-ling's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia dates the Shanghai classes to 1939 and calls them among the first yoga classes taught in China, held at the house of Soong Mei-ling, Madame Chiang Kai-shek; Hinduism Today independently names Madame Chiang Kai-shek's house. The superlative is narrowed here to modern postural yoga, since older Chinese bodily disciplines long predate it. The pin is the canonical Shanghai coordinate inherited from madame_chiang_kai_shek.journey.json.
stops.campa: Her husband is posted to Shanghai, and she arrives in the treaty port with a teacher's instruction and no students. She finds them at the top: Soong Mei-ling, wife of the Generalissimo, opens her own house for the classes. Foreign women and Chinese women lie down on the floor of that house and are taught to breathe, in a city where the Japanese army already holds everything outside the foreign concessions. It is the first sustained teaching of modern postural yoga in China.
suggested_refs: The Soong residence, Shanghai, venue of the first classes

stops.name: Shanghai, teaching through the occupation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That she went on teaching in Shanghai through the war years follows from the attested 1939 start and the attested 1947 departure, but no source reached this pass documents the intervening years directly. The free classes in orphanages are dossier material, unconfirmed. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Japanese take the concessions in December 1941 and the foreign city she taught in stops existing as a legal space. She stays, and goes on teaching. The dossier says she taught orphans for nothing in these years; nothing reachable confirms it, and it is exactly the kind of detail that attaches itself to a person after they become famous. What is certain is that she is in occupied Shanghai for the duration, a Czechoslovak passport holder from a country that has also stopped existing.
suggested_refs: Shanghai foreign-resident registrations under Japanese occupation, 1942-1945, not consulted
sources: research dossier synthesis, unconfirmed for the orphanages

stops.name: Shanghai, widowed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact and year only: en.wikipedia gives Jan Strakaty's death as 1946. No source reached this pass gives a place. The pin is the household's Shanghai address and is not an attested place of death; the research pool's suggestion of 'Europe (traveling)' is likewise unsupported and is not used. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Jan Strakaty dies in the sixteenth year of the marriage. The year is attested and the place is not. Where he died is recorded in nothing that can be checked, which is its own kind of fact about a marriage conducted across four countries and a world war. She is forty-six, a widow, holding a passport from a state now inside the Soviet sphere, in a city where the Chinese civil war is about to make her property worthless. Everything that had placed her since 1930 is gone inside a single year.
suggested_refs: Czechoslovak consular death registers, 1946, not consulted

stops.name: Allahabad, the first book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book: the Bauman Rare Books catalogue records Yoga: The Technique of Health and Happiness, Allahabad, Kitabistan, 1948, bylined 'Eugenie Strakaty (Indira Devi),' in blue cloth with a photographic frontispiece portrait, seventeen plates of asanas and two line drawings. The 1946 composition date is unsourced. The stop is dated 1947 to place the manuscript on the return journey that precedes the sailing to San Francisco; the imprint is 1948. Note that Open Library dates the same title to 1984, which is a catalogue error against Bauman's first edition.
stops.campa: Widowed, she returns to India and writes the book down: what Krishnamacharya taught, in English, for people who will never see Mysore. Kitabistan of Allahabad prints it in blue cloth, with a portrait frontispiece, seventeen plates of asanas and two line drawings. A rare-books catalogue still lists a first edition of it; one library catalogue dates the same book to 1984, thirty-six years late. The name on the title page is not yet the one the world will use. It reads Eugenie Strakaty, and then, in brackets after it, Indira Devi.
suggested_refs: Yoga: The Technique of Health and Happiness (Allahabad: Kitabistan, 1948), first edition
sources: baumanrarebooks.com listing 115333, Devi, Yoga: The Technique of Health and Happiness

stops.name: San Francisco, off the troop transport
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1947 arrival in the United States, given by Time and by the Dawn obituary; Time records her arriving with six thousand dollars in savings. The ship's name, the USS General W. H. Gordon, comes from en.wikipedia and the dossier and was not re-verified against a passenger manifest. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: She crosses the Pacific on a troop transport, one more displaced European on a ship built to move soldiers, and lands in San Francisco at forty-eight with six thousand dollars and no profession the country recognises. She has done this before, in Berlin at twenty-one and in Bombay at twenty-nine. The procedure is known to her: arrive, look at what the place wants, and be the person who has it. What California wants has no name yet in English. She spends a year in the country before she opens a room.
stops.quote: The only thing left to do was to begin anew.
stops.quote_source: Her own writing, quoted in Time, 'The Woman Who Hooked Hollywood Stars on Yoga' (2015). Time does not name the book or page.
suggested_refs: Passenger manifest of the USS General W. H. Gordon, Shanghai to San Francisco, 1947, not located

stops.name: 8806 Sunset Boulevard, the studio
stops.date_confidence: attested that she opened a dedicated yoga studio on Sunset Boulevard in 1948, described by en.wikipedia as the first in Los Angeles; the Dawn obituary calls it the first in the United States, which the research dossier itself flags as promotional overstatement. The street number is a bibliographic detail not re-verified this pass. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: She rents a room on Sunset Boulevard and teaches in a sari, and what she teaches is not what Mysore taught her. The regimen is softened, slowed, aimed at relaxation and at bodies that sit in cars and offices. Studio secretaries come, and factory workers, and then Gloria Swanson, Greta Garbo and Eva Gabor, and the newspapers arrive behind the names. The claim that it is the first yoga studio in America is a claim her own publicity made and her biographer disputes.
suggested_refs: The studio premises at 8806 Sunset Boulevard, West Hollywood

stops.name: Hollywood Hills, the Huxleys' table
stops.date_confidence: attested: Time reports her visits to Aldous and Maria Huxley, the conversations about diet and pesticides, and her later quoting of Huxley on nonattachment, and places her within the circle around the hostess Bernardine Fritz. The year is set to 1949 to order the segment; Time gives the late 1940s.
stops.campa: Aldous and Maria Huxley keep a house in the hills where the conversation runs to diet, pesticides in food, mescaline, and what a person is supposed to do with attention. Devi sits at that table. She quotes Huxley on nonattachment in her own books afterwards. Around that table is a Hollywood that has already decided the East has something and has no clear idea what, and she is the only person in the house who was taught by anyone. She is fifty years old and eleven years out of Mysore.
suggested_refs: The salon of Bernardine Fritz, Los Angeles
Aldous Huxley on nonattachment, quoted in Devi's own books

stops.name: Los Angeles, Forever Young and a second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 1953 for both the publication of Forever Young, Forever Healthy and the marriage to Dr. Sigfrid Knauer. Open Library confirms Forever Young, Forever Healthy, 1953, in four editions, but records no publisher, so the attribution to Prentice-Hall carried in the research pool is dropped here as unsourced.
stops.campa: The second book sells on a promise the first did not make: not health, exactly, but the arrest of age, from a woman of fifty-four who looks like an argument for her own thesis. The same year she marries Sigfrid Knauer, a doctor some fifteen years her senior with money and land. She is now an American author with an American husband and a Russian birth certificate she does not use. The dossier claim that Elizabeth Arden's salons took up her methods could not be confirmed at all.
suggested_refs: Forever Young, Forever Healthy (1953), four catalogued editions

stops.name: Los Angeles, the name made legal
stops.date_confidence: attested only as mid-1950s. en.wikipedia says verbatim: 'In the mid-1950s she was granted American citizenship and changed her legal name to Indra Devi.' No source reached this pass narrows it to 1955, and the date here is a placeholder inside the attested range. Yoga for Americans, 1959, is attested by en.wikipedia and by Open Library, which records five editions and an ebook but no publisher.
stops.campa: She takes American citizenship, and on the same papers she stops being Eugenia Peterson. The screen name a Bombay studio gave her in 1930 becomes the name of a United States citizen. Four years later she publishes Yoga for Americans, which is precisely what she has spent a decade manufacturing: a version of the discipline that a suburban household can perform without believing anything in particular. It sells for decades. Five editions of it are catalogued, and an ebook, and not one catalogue entry names the publisher.
suggested_refs: Yoga for Americans (1959), five catalogued editions and an ebook
United States naturalisation and name-change records, mid-1950s, not located

stops.name: Moscow, back inside the Union
stops.date_confidence: attested that she visited the USSR in 1960 and met the ministers Andrei Gromyko and Alexei Kosygin: en.wikipedia. Nearly every other detail in circulation fails: no source reached this pass supports a Leningrad leg, a Finland routing, a companion named Balu Krishna, the ambassador K. P. S. Menon, or a reception at the Hotel Sovetskaya, and Time's Moscow material concerns a 1990s trip, not this one. A contradiction is left standing: Hinduism Today claims the visit won legal status for teaching yoga in Russia, which the scholarship regards as greatly exaggerated, since Soviet yoga stayed restricted until perestroika. The city pin is used rather than the disputed hotel.
stops.campa: Forty years after she left it, she comes back to the country as an American citizen with an Indian name, and is received by ministers of the Soviet government. She explains to them that yoga is a method and not a religion, which is the formula Krishnamacharya gave her and the only formula that could have been said in that room. Her obituarists will claim she legalised yoga in Russia that week. She did not. It stayed underground for another twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: Soviet foreign ministry records of the 1960 reception, not consulted

stops.name: Rancho Cuchuma, the teacher-training years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the purchase and the year: en.wikipedia records the Tecate ranch bought in 1961 and the operation closed in 1977, a span of sixteen years. The purchase price, the deed and any enrolment records remain unlocated. The coordinate is the town of Tecate, consistent with a site at the foot of Mount Cuchuma.
stops.campa: Knauer buys a ranch below Mount Cuchuma on the Mexican side of the border, an hour and a half from San Diego, and Devi turns it into a school for teachers. Californians cross to be certified. For sixteen years the output of this place is not students but instructors, who go home certified and open rooms of their own under their own names. There is no monastery here and no scripture, only a ranch and a certificate. No deed, price or enrolment book from those years has been found.
stops.quote: Movements in yoga are harmonious, slow, soft, plastic, relaxed, always conscious...
stops.quote_source: Hinduism Today, 'Indra Devi's Legacy' (Oct-Dec 2002), section 'In Her Own Sweet Words'. The ellipsis is the magazine's; the passage is probably truncated from a longer original that the magazine does not name.
suggested_refs: The Indra Devi Foundation teacher-training centre at Rancho Cuchuma, Tecate, Baja California

stops.name: Puttaparthi, Prasanthi Nilayam
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia and Hinduism Today both date her devotion to Sathya Sai Baba from 1966 and record the reframing of her teaching as Sai Yoga. The coordinate is the ashram's own, corrected from the rounded figure carried in the research pool. Salon's 2001 reporting on the allegations against Sai Baba does not mention Devi.
stops.campa: At sixty-seven she meets Sathya Sai Baba at his ashram in Andhra Pradesh and becomes his devotee, and the method that had been carefully stripped of religion for American consumption acquires a god. She publicises his teachings and his miracles. Her own name for what she teaches becomes Sai Yoga. The students she trained in California had been promised a technique with nothing metaphysical attached, and not all of them are able to follow her here. She keeps both, the technique and the god, and goes on teaching them together for the next thirty-six years.
suggested_refs: Prasanthi Nilayam ashram, Puttaparthi
Later allegations against Sathya Sai Baba, reported in Salon, 25 July 2001

stops.name: Tecate, the gate closed
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia records the Tecate operation closed in 1977 and the move to Bangalore the same year. Knauer's illness as the reason is consistent with the sources but is stated explicitly by none of them.
stops.campa: She is seventy-seven and Knauer is failing. The teacher-training centre shuts after sixteen years, the students disperse, and the ranch below the mountain stops being an institution. There is no succession, no appointed heir, no incorporated school left standing in North America with her name over the door. The Indra Devi Foundation, which had meant this ranch and these buildings, stops meaning anything with an address. It is the fourth country she has left, and she sells nothing to anyone before she goes.

stops.name: Bangalore, nursing years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move and year: en.wikipedia records the move to Bangalore in 1977. The end of this period is inferred from es.wikipedia's 1983 departure for Sri Lanka. That she chose Bangalore for its nearness to Sai Baba's orbit is inference, not a sourced statement. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: They settle in Bangalore, within reach of Puttaparthi, and for six years the most publicised yoga teacher in the western hemisphere is a woman in her late seventies caring for a dying husband in a South Indian city. Nothing is published and no school is founded. This is the longest stretch of her adult life in which she is not building something, and what she did in that house between 1977 and 1983 is not recorded in anything reachable; the institutional biographies give the whole period a sentence. Knauer takes six years to die.

stops.name: Sri Lanka, Knauer dies
stops.date_confidence: attested by three independent sources that Sigfrid Knauer died in Sri Lanka in 1984: en.wikipedia, es.wikipedia and Hinduism Today; es.wikipedia dates their travel there to 1983. No source specifies where in Sri Lanka, so the coordinate is Colombo used as a country marker, not an attested place of death. Some secondary accounts misdate the death to 1977, confusing it with the closing of the Tecate centre; all three sources here contradict that, and it is set aside rather than left open.
stops.campa: They travel to Sri Lanka and Knauer dies there, close to ninety. Where on the island is not recorded, and no source reached this pass names a town or a date inside the year. She is eighty-four and twice widowed, with no house in any country she holds a passport from, no institution, and no students within six thousand miles. Her heart, which three countries of doctors could not name a cure for in 1932, has outlasted both husbands. She has been to Argentina once, two years earlier, to give a seminar.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first visit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit and the year: Hinduism Today records the 1982 Argentine visit and says she fell in love with the country and its people. The seminar, the television appearance and the extraordinary public demand that followed are institutional self-description from the foundation and are not independently verified. The pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate carried by victoria_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: She comes to Argentina at eighty-three to give a seminar, in the last year of the military dictatorship, in a city full of people who cannot say in public what has happened to their families. She goes on television. Whatever she is offering, the response is out of proportion to it, and the foundation's own account of the size of that response cannot be checked against a newspaper. No Argentine press notice of the seminar or the broadcast has been located. She goes away and starts arranging her affairs.
suggested_refs: Argentine television broadcast of the 1982 seminar, not located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, settling for good
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives 1985 for the permanent settlement in Buenos Aires. A contradiction is left standing: Hinduism Today's chronology implies the relocation followed directly on Knauer's death in 1984, and both years are in circulation. Her formulation about the three countries is reported by Hinduism Today.
stops.campa: She moves to Buenos Aires and does not leave again. Russia, she says, is the country of her birth; India is the country of her spirit; Argentina is the country of her love. She is eighty-six years old and has just chosen, freely and for the first time, where she is going to live. The year of the move is given as 1985 by one source and implied as 1984 by another, and both are in circulation. Every previous address was set for her by a war, a marriage, or a man's money. Porteños call her Mataji, which means mother.
stops.quote: I'm just a person. I don't pretend to be.
stops.quote_source: Reported as something she would always say, relayed by her biographer Michelle Goldberg in YogaCityNYC, 'Breaking Myths: The Story of Indra Devi' (20 June 2016). A habitual remark, not a dated utterance.
sources: yogacitynyc.com, 'Breaking Myths: The Story of Indra Devi'

stops.name: Montevideo, president of honour
stops.date_confidence: attested with a caveat on the city. en.wikipedia gives 'Elected president of honour, International Yoga Federation: 1987 (Montevideo, Uruguay)'; es.wikipedia corroborates the year and the country but does not name the city. SciELO Argentina attributes the founding of the Federacion Internacional de Yoga to Devi together with Swami Maitreyananda, that is Fernando Estevez Griego, and Vayuananda, that is Carlos Ovidio Trotta. Organisation names are rendered inconsistently across the institutional sources.
stops.campa: Across the river in Montevideo a federation of yoga teachers makes her its president of honour. She is eighty-eight, has been teaching for forty-nine years, and has never before held an office in any organisation, having spent her life founding things she then walked away from. The federation is named differently in every account that mentions it, and the sources naming her co-founders do not agree on who they were. She accepts the title and goes back across the river to teach.
suggested_refs: Federacion Internacional de Yoga, founded with Swami Maitreyananda and Vayuananda

stops.name: Panama City, the colonel who broke ranks
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the weakest stop in this file. What is attested: Roberto Diaz Herrera, forced into retirement in June 1987, publicly broke with the Panamanian Defense Forces command and said by his own account that he did so at the behest of Sathya Sai Baba. What is not: Devi's own role. The introduction through the Argentine singer Piero, the invitation to Panama at Defense Forces expense, and the demonstrations she is said to have given rest on the dossier alone. The pin is inherited from manuel_noriega.journey.json, whose file contains no mention of Diaz Herrera, Piero or Devi, a documented gap rather than a corroboration.
stops.campa: The second-ranking officer of the Panamanian Defense Forces, forced into retirement, calls a press conference and detonates his own regime, and afterwards says he acted at the instruction of an Indian guru. That guru is Devi's. Two years later the Americans invade. The chain by which an eighty-eight-year-old yoga teacher in Buenos Aires is said to reach a colonel in Panama City runs through an Argentine folk singer, and is documented in nothing that could be reached this pass.
suggested_refs: Princeton Latin American Ephemera Collections, Diaz Herrera folder, not consulted
CIA FOIA request F-2010-01317, filed by Michelle Goldberg
sources: research dossier synthesis, unconfirmed for Devi's role

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Fundacion
stops.date_confidence: attested for the foundation, with the founders disputed. Indra Devi International gives 1988 as the founding year and records that the Fundacion ran until 2020, when Iana and David Lifar transitioned it into a virtual school; Hinduism Today names David Lifar, husband of her disciple Iana Lifar, as co-founder. SciELO Argentina instead attributes the co-founding to Devi with Swami Maitreyananda and does not mention the Lifars. Both attributions are recorded; neither is resolved here.
stops.campa: The Fundacion Indra Devi, Yoga, Arte y Ciencia de Vida, opens in Buenos Aires with Iana and David Lifar, and at eighty-nine she finally builds the institution she declined to build in California, in Mexico and in India. It trains teachers, prints a periodical and convenes congresses. Who exactly stood beside her at the founding is told two different ways by two sources that both had reason to know, and both of them name her first. It runs until 2020.
stops.quote: I do not belong to any religion. Everything is between God and myself.
stops.quote_source: Hinduism Today, 'Indra Devi's Legacy' (Oct-Dec 2002), main text. The magazine names no underlying book or interview.
suggested_refs: Fundacion Indra Devi, Yoga, Arte y Ciencia de Vida, 1988-2020

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first Argentine Yoga Congress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the event and her role: SciELO Argentina records a first Argentine Yoga Congress in the late 1980s presided over by Devi together with Swami Maitreyananda, and treats it as pivotal in consolidating the country's modern yoga lineages. The city is inferred, not sourced: the article does not say where the congress was held, and the Buenos Aires pin is an assumption. The year is likewise placed inside the late 1980s to order the segment.
stops.campa: The country's yoga teachers convene for the first time and she presides, with Swami Maitreyananda beside her. An academic genealogy written thirty years later dates the consolidation of Argentina's modern yoga lineages to this gathering, and credits her with the formula she carried out of Mysore fifty years earlier: that this is a method for physical, mental and spiritual development, and not a religion. Where the congress met is not recorded in that article.
stops.quote: Yoga is an art and science of living. Yoga means union, in all its significances and dimensions. Through a certain amount of physical and mental disciplines we can learn how to stay healthy, alert, receptive and to improve our perception of the external world in order to feel internally harmonized, with a better life condition and spiritual balance.
stops.quote_source: Hinduism Today, 'Indra Devi's Legacy' (Oct-Dec 2002), section 'In Her Own Sweet Words'. The magazine names no underlying book.
suggested_refs: SciELO Argentina, genealogy of modern yoga in Argentina, S1853-70812018000100005

stops.name: Riga, ninety-one years later
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The return to Riga in May 1990, as part of a Soviet tour that also took in Leningrad and Moscow, is dossier material and was not independently confirmed this pass. What is independently attested is a Moscow trip in the 1990s, reported by Time. The Riga leg specifically has no reachable source.
stops.campa: She returns to the city she was born in, at ninety-one, in the last months before Latvia leaves the Soviet Union. The house is not recorded, and neither is whether she looked for it. She was twenty-one when she left this city. Nothing in the reachable record says what she did in Riga or who met her there. The visit is asserted by her foundation and by the retellings that follow it, and by no document at all, which is the condition of most of the last decade of her life.
suggested_refs: Latvian press coverage of the May 1990 visit, not located

stops.name: Moscow, lotus position on television
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Time attests a Moscow trip in the 1990s in the company of David and Iana Lifar but gives no year and names no programme; the appearance on Vladimir Molchanov's Do i posle polunochi is dossier material. The year 1990 is therefore not established. The encounter with a woman claiming kinship, and her reply, are reported by Time from Michelle Goldberg's biography.
stops.campa: Soviet television puts a ninety-one-year-old woman in lotus position in front of the largest audience she has ever had, in the country that expelled her family seventy years earlier. A woman in Moscow comes forward claiming kinship, and Devi will not take her up. Whether the claim was true is established nowhere, and the woman's name is not recorded. The programme that carried the appearance is named by her foundation and by no broadcast listing anyone has produced.
stops.quote: I try to live in the eternal now. This lady belongs to my past.
stops.quote_source: Reported in Time, 'The Woman Who Hooked Hollywood Stars on Yoga' (2015), drawing on Michelle Goldberg's biography The Goddess Pose.
suggested_refs: Do i posle polunochi, presented by Vladimir Molchanov, Soviet television; broadcast date unconfirmed
sources: research dossier synthesis, unconfirmed for the programme

stops.name: United Nations Headquarters, the invited lecture
stops.date_confidence: institutional testimony only. Indra Devi International states verbatim that she was specially invited to give a lecture at United Nations headquarters in June 1992. No UN programme, transcript or press record corroborating it was located this pass, and the claim is carried here on the foundation's authority alone.
stops.campa: Her foundation records that she is invited to speak at the headquarters of the United Nations in June 1992, at ninety-three. The foundation is precise about the month and says nothing about the room. Either the event happened and left no reachable trace, which is ordinary for a guest speaker in a building that hosts hundreds of them every year, or it grew in the telling. The claim stands here on her foundation's authority and nothing else. No programme, transcript or press notice of that lecture has been found.
stops.quote: Nonviolence is one of the keys of yoga, and we should begin it by ourselves...
stops.quote_source: Hinduism Today, 'Indra Devi's Legacy' (Oct-Dec 2002), section 'In Her Own Sweet Words'. The ellipsis is the magazine's and the passage is probably truncated; no underlying text is named.
suggested_refs: UN Headquarters programme records, June 1992, not located

stops.name: Palacio del Congreso, the Women's Day honour
stops.date_confidence: institutional testimony. Indra Devi International states verbatim that on 8 March 1999, for International Women's Day, the Congress of the Nation honoured her. No congressional record was located this pass. Note a cross-lens inconsistency in the research pool, where the identical event was tagged both attested and unverified. The coordinate is the Palacio del Congreso, corrected from a figure in the pool that pointed at the Plaza de Mayo instead.
stops.campa: The Argentine Congress honours her on International Women's Day, for work in the promotion of love, light and peace, three months before her hundredth birthday. She is a Latvian-born, Russian-raised, Indian-named American citizen being decorated by the legislature of a fourth country. Whether the session left a record in the congressional archive is not something this pass could establish; only her foundation's account of it can be read. She is ninety-nine.
stops.quote: We women must listen to our inner voice. It is easier for women to do this as they are not afraid to say what they feel. We must keep both our femininity and our strength. Men have to descend from their pedestal and learn how to be more broadminded and spiritual.
stops.quote_source: Hinduism Today, 'Indra Devi's Legacy' (Oct-Dec 2002), section 'In Her Own Sweet Words'. The full passage as printed there; BrainyQuote's shorter copy is downstream of this article, not independent corroboration.
suggested_refs: Diario de Sesiones of the Argentine Congress, 8 March 1999, not consulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, one hundred years old
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the celebration. The birth date of 12 May 1899 is attested; the reported attendance of more than three thousand people at the centenary festivities comes only from the foundation's own institutional account, and no press coverage confirming the figure was located this pass.
stops.campa: A hundred years to the day after a bank director's daughter was born in Riga, several thousand people are reported to fill a hall in Buenos Aires for her birthday. The Fundacion counts the crowd at more than three thousand; no newspaper does, and no account names the hall. Nobody present has known her longer than seventeen years, and she is the only person in the hall who remembers the Russian Empire. She teaches that week, receives visitors all day, and is photographed until the light goes.
suggested_refs: Argentine press coverage of the May 1999 centenary, not located
sources: Fundacion Indra Devi institutional history, via the research dossier

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last morning
stops.date_confidence: attested: Hinduism Today, the Dawn obituary and Time all report the death in Buenos Aires at 102, seventeen days short of 103, and Hinduism Today reports a stroke in February 2002 that paralysed her right side. A minor discrepancy stands: Dawn's dateline gives 26 April against the 25 April carried elsewhere. Contemporary obituaries note that no official cause of death was disclosed.
stops.campa: A stroke in February takes her right side, and she does not teach again. She dies on the twenty-fifth of April, seventeen days short of a hundred and three, in the city she chose at eighty-six out of every city she had ever lived in. Her devotees keep watch over the body for three days without burying it, because she had taught them that the soul takes three days to come loose. The vigil runs the full three days, in a flat in Buenos Aires. No official cause of death is given out.
stops.quote: Mataji abandonó su cuerpo físico el 25 de abril de 2002, próxima a cumplir 103 años.
stops.quote_source: Indra Devi International, indradevi-international.net.ar: 'Mataji left her physical body on 25 April 2002, close to turning 103.'

stops.name: Rio de la Plata, the ashes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact: Hinduism Today reports that her body was cremated and her ashes scattered in the Rio de la Plata. The exact date and point are not recorded, and the coordinate is a plausible position in the estuary off Buenos Aires; the research pool carried two figures for this event some thirty-five kilometres apart, and the nearer one is used in both places. There is no grave, marker, statue or plaque for her in Riga, at Tecate, or anywhere else that could be located this pass.
stops.campa: She is cremated by Hindu rite and the ashes go into the Rio de la Plata, the brown estuary the width of a sea, off the city she called the country of her love. There is no grave. There is no stone in Riga, none at Tecate, none on Sunset Boulevard. What she leaves behind is scattered students and one foundation, not a lineage with a seat, and the students scatter again as they had scattered from Hollywood and from Tecate. No monument, marker or plaque to her has been located anywhere.
suggested_refs: Michelle Goldberg, The Goddess Pose: The Audacious Life of Indra Devi (Knopf, 2015)
sources: yogacitynyc.com, 'Breaking Myths: The Story of Indra Devi'
